resource: What a URL such as `myDomain.com/api/customers` names; every http request has a verb that determines its intention toward it (slide 3). See [PUT replaces, PATCH updates, and only PUT is idempotent](#/comp4537-l6/idempotency-put-patch-post).
PUT: Replacing an object entirely with something new; PUT is idempotent (slide 3). See [PUT replaces, PATCH updates, and only PUT is idempotent](#/comp4537-l6/idempotency-put-patch-post).
PATCH: Updating only a property of an object (slide 3). See [PUT replaces, PATCH updates, and only PUT is idempotent](#/comp4537-l6/idempotency-put-patch-post).
idempotent|idempotency: Can be applied multiple times without changing the result; calling PUT once or several times has the same effect, successive identical POSTs may place an order several times (slide 3). See [PUT replaces, PATCH updates, and only PUT is idempotent](#/comp4537-l6/idempotency-put-patch-post).
first-class function|first-class functio: In JS a function can receive another function as a parameter, as `bar(foo)` does (slide 4). See [Functions as values, callbacks, and why a function returns only one thing](#/comp4537-l6/callbacks-and-first-class-functions).
callback|callbacks: "here is the function to call once you are done", passed in with the arguments, as `myDisplayer` is in `myCalculator(5, 5, myDisplayer)` (slide 5). See [Functions as values, callbacks, and why a function returns only one thing](#/comp4537-l6/callbacks-and-first-class-functions).
asynchronous|async operation: An operation whose result comes later; any communication via the net is asynchronous, so microservices calling each other are (slide 8). See [Functions as values, callbacks, and why a function returns only one thing](#/comp4537-l6/callbacks-and-first-class-functions).
callback hell: Nesting each next asynchronous call inside the previous one's callback, as `myFunc2` inside `myFunc1` (slide 40). See [async functions return promises, await waits for one](#/comp4537-l6/async-await).
Promise|promise: An object used for asynchronous computations; it represents a single asynchronous operation that hasn't completed yet, but is expected in the future (slide 16). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
pending: The state of a promise before it is settled; you don't know yet if you will get the raise (slide 13). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
fulfilled|resolved: The state after `resolve()` is called first; older Chrome shows it as "resolved" (slides 13, 37). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
rejected: The state after `reject()` is called first; the boss withholds the raise (slide 13). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
settled: Fulfilled or rejected; once settled, the state does not change (slides 14, 24). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
promise state|promise status: The same concept, the condition of a Promise object: pending, fulfilled or rejected (slide 35). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
executor|executer: The function passed to the Promise constructor; it gets references to resolve and reject and is executed immediately upon creation of the promise object (slides 16, 17). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
resolve: The function the executor receives first; calling it changes the promise to fulfilled and creates the promise's value (slides 17, 18). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
reject: The function the executor receives second; calling it changes the promise to rejected (slides 17, 18). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
handler|handlers: The functions passed to `.then()`; they receive the promise's value and run asynchronously, mutually exclusive, and only once (slides 17, 18). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
eager: Promises start executing the moment a new Promise is constructed (slide 19). See [Pending, fulfilled, rejected, and the executor that runs immediately](#/comp4537-l6/promise-states-and-the-executor).
settle once|settle-once: After a promise is settled, later resolve or reject calls do nothing ("Hi" is logged only once) (slides 17, 24). See [Synchronous code first, then the handlers: Examples 1 to 6](#/comp4537-l6/ordering-part-1).
microtask|microtask queue: Where promise handlers wait; they run only after the current call stack finishes, not after "all code in the program" (slide 17). See [Synchronous code first, then the handlers: Examples 1 to 6](#/comp4537-l6/ordering-part-1).
call stack|current call stack: The synchronous code now running; promise handlers wait only for it to unwind (slide 17). See [Synchronous code first, then the handlers: Examples 1 to 6](#/comp4537-l6/ordering-part-1).
Promise.resolve|Promise.reject: Shortcuts to manually create an already resolved or rejected promise (slide 25). See [Synchronous code first, then the handlers: Examples 1 to 6](#/comp4537-l6/ordering-part-1).
macrotask|timer queue: Where a `setTimeout` callback waits; it runs after the microtasks, even with 0 ms (slide 28, computed order). See [Microtasks before timers: Examples 7 to 11 and the harder shapes](#/comp4537-l6/ordering-part-2).
chaining|promise chain: Calling `.then()` on the promise another `.then()` returns; the then() method returns a Promise, that's why we can chain promises (slide 26). See [Synchronous code first, then the handlers: Examples 1 to 6](#/comp4537-l6/ordering-part-1).
then|.then: The method whose first argument runs when the promise is resolved and receives the result, and whose second runs when it is rejected and receives the error (slide 43). See [then, catch and finally: return fulfils, throw rejects](#/comp4537-l6/chaining-then-catch-finally).
catch|.catch: `.catch(f)` is the same as `.then(null, f)`; used when we're interested only in errors (slide 46). See [then, catch and finally: return fulfils, throw rejects](#/comp4537-l6/chaining-then-catch-finally).
finally|.finally: `.finally(f)` is similar to `.then(f, f)`: it always runs when the promise is settled, be it resolve or reject (slide 48). See [then, catch and finally: return fulfils, throw rejects](#/comp4537-l6/chaining-then-catch-finally).
unhandled rejection|Uncaught (in promise: The console error for a rejected promise with no rejection handler, e.g. `Uncaught (in promise) Whoops!` (slides 29, 39, 51). See [then, catch and finally: return fulfils, throw rejects](#/comp4537-l6/chaining-then-catch-finally).
async function|async: A function declared async automatically returns a promise (slide 52). See [async functions return promises, await waits for one](#/comp4537-l6/async-await).
await: Used inside async functions to wait for a promise to resolve or reject (slide 52). See [async functions return promises, await waits for one](#/comp4537-l6/async-await).
readyState: The XHR property; 0 UNSENT, 1 OPENED, 2 HEADERS_RECEIVED, 3 LOADING, 4 DONE (slide 55). See [async functions return promises, await waits for one](#/comp4537-l6/async-await).
HEADERS_RECEIVED: ReadyState 2: send() has been called, and the headers of the response are available (slide 55). See [async functions return promises, await waits for one](#/comp4537-l6/async-await).
